claim: Face recognition is reported in animals from a number of distinct evolutionary lineages.
source: Among all of the individual recognition (IR) systems, face recognition is one of the most specific abilities, and is reported in animals from a number of distinct evolutionary lineages (Kendrick and Baldwin, 1987; McKone et al., 2007; Van der Velden et al., 2008, Coulon et al., 2009; Racca et al., 2010; Sheehan and Tibbetts, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Human infants are hypothesised to be attracted to faces innately.

claim: A familiar face can be individuated in 250 ms.

claim: Prosopagnosia is a neuropsychological disorder in which individuals are unable to recognise faces but have no difficulty in recognising individuals by other modalities or in discriminating non-face objects.
source: Studies of a neuropsychological disorder known as prosopagnosia or face blindness, in which individuals are unable to recognise faces but have no difficulty in recognising individuals by other modalities (such as voice) or in discriminating non-face objects (Meadows, 1974; Behrmann et al., 2005), have shown that facial recognition proceeds through specific cognitive and neural pathways (Valentine, 1988; McKone et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Facial recognition proceeds through specific cognitive and neural pathways.

claim: The increase in recognition difficulty associated with inversion of faces is greater than that for the inversion of other types of visual stimuli.

claim: The face-inversion effect indirectly indicates that faces are perceived configurally rather than only by specific features.
source: The so-called face-inversion effect indirectly indicates that faces are perceived configurally rather than only by specific features (such as the eyes, nose, or mouth), and that once inverted, such a global configuration is difficult to match and passes through routes which are used for recognising other objects (Bartlett and Searcy, 1993; Haxby et al., 1999; Boutsen et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Once inverted, the global configuration of faces is difficult to match and passes through routes which are used for recognising other objects.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Thatcher illusion is found in both humans and monkeys.
source: Likewise, the Thatcher illusion found in both humans (Thompson, 1980) and monkeys (Adachi et al., 2009; Dahl et al., 2010), in which the eyes and mouth are inverted relative to the face, becomes difficult to detect when upside down, further demonstrating that configural perception is interrupted when orientation is inverted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The face inversion effect has been identified in some non-human primates and in sheep.
source: The face inversion effect is the method most widely used in animals to test whether faces may be processed specifically, and researchers have identified this ability in some non-human primates (Overman and Doty, 1982; Tomonaga, 1994; Parr et al., 1998; Vermeire and Hamilton, 1998; Neiworth et al., 2007) and in sheep (Kendrick et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Some monkeys failed to show oriented-specific face-processing.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Many studies on monkey face processing lacked the use of non-face signals as controls, making it difficult to interpret the results.

claim: Specialised neural systems for face recognition have been found in some non-human primates and in sheep.
